It establishes that candidate output is rising extraordinarily quickly in several research channels, that disclosed AI participation is rising extraordinarily quickly in mathematics, and that major conferences report operational consequences associated with both submission volume and AI-mediated behavior. Moving from those observations to a causal productivity effect requires eliminating several alternative explanations.

The first is also the simplest: **the research system was already expanding before contemporary generative AI existed**. ICLR grew from 67 conference-track submissions in 2013 to more than 265 in 2016 and then to 1,591 in 2019.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-early-history][^the-research-explosion-iclr-intermediate-history] ChatGPT's public research preview began only on November 30, 2022.[^the-research-explosion-chatgpt-release] Generative AI therefore cannot explain the origin of ICLR's exponential-looking long-run trajectory. Any adequate account must begin with mechanisms already operating during the preceding decade and ask whether generative AI later changed their magnitude rather than assuming that it created them.

The broader publication record reinforces that point. Stanford's 2026 AI Index, using OpenAlex and an automated computer-science ontology to identify AI research, estimates that worldwide AI publications increased from approximately 102,000 in 2013 to about 258,000 in 2024. AI's share of computer-science publications rose from roughly 21% to about 41% over the same interval.[^the-research-explosion-ai-index-publications] Although bibliographic classification is not equivalent to conference submission accounting, the direction is clear: the research domain itself underwent a large secular expansion long before generative AI could plausibly have become a ubiquitous research assistant.

One component of that expansion is growth in the population participating in machine-learning research. ICLR's own attendance statistics report 2,600 participants in 2019, 3,758 in 2023, 6,533 in 2024, 11,137 in 2025, and 9,954 in 2026.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2026-fact-sheet] Attendance is an imperfect proxy for the number of active researchers because geography, venue capacity, travel cost, visa availability, virtual access, and conference attractiveness all affect participation. It nevertheless provides independent evidence that the community around the conference has become much larger. A larger research population can generate more papers even if output per researcher remains unchanged.

The ICLR submission curve, however, has grown still faster than this attendance proxy. Reported submissions increased from 1,591 in 2019 to 19,525 in 2026, a factor of approximately **12.3**, whereas reported conference participation increased from 2,600 to 9,954, a factor of approximately **3.8**.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-intermediate-history][^the-research-explosion-iclr-2026-fact-sheet] These ratios should not be interpreted as estimates of per-researcher productivity: conference attendance and submitting authors are different populations, papers have multiple authors, and both measurements are affected by changing institutional conditions. They do show why demographic growth alone cannot simply be assumed to explain the submission trajectory. Distinguishing population growth from increasing output per researcher requires author-level data rather than attendance counts.

A second explanation is an increase in the **number of research opportunities**. AI is unusual because the technology that may be increasing research productivity is simultaneously generating the phenomena being researched. New foundation models, architectures, training methods, evaluation techniques, datasets, applications, safety problems, alignment methods, inference systems, hardware constraints, agent architectures, and theoretical questions continuously create new objects of study. ICLR's current call spans not only representation learning and optimization but language, vision, audio, reinforcement learning, robotics, healthcare, biology, sustainability, economics, neuroscience, physical science, safety, privacy, datasets, infrastructure, software, and hardware.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-call] An expanding technological frontier can therefore increase submission volume without any increase in researchers' ability to produce a given piece of research.

This creates a particularly important endogeneity problem. AI can increase publication output through at least two conceptually distinct channels:

1. **AI as the object of research:** rapid technological development creates more questions worth investigating.
2. **AI as an input to research:** AI tools reduce the resources required to investigate a question and produce a research artifact.

The ICLR submission curve contains both effects and cannot separate them. A surge in papers evaluating new models, proposing inference methods, studying alignment failures, or applying AI to new scientific domains may occur because there is simply more AI-related reality to investigate. Using that same surge as evidence that AI tools make researchers more productive would therefore confound the independent variable with the subject being measured.

A third explanation is **venue substitution**. Growth at one conference need not represent proportional growth in the total quantity of research. ICLR can gain submissions because its scientific scope expands, because its prestige changes, because authors redirect papers from journals or competing conferences, or because work that previously would have been distributed across several communities becomes concentrated in machine-learning venues. Conference statistics measure demand directed toward a particular evaluation institution, not the complete production of the underlying research population.

The broader evidence assembled earlier in this article makes pure venue substitution unlikely to explain the entire phenomenon, because large increases are visible at multiple major conferences and on arXiv. It nevertheless remains relevant when interpreting any individual conference series. The nearly 300-fold ICLR increase should not be read as evidence that machine-learning research as a whole became 300 times more productive.

A fourth mechanism is **general research infrastructure rather than generative AI specifically**. Over the period covered by the ICLR series, researchers gained access to mature open-source ML frameworks, public model repositories, benchmark suites, reusable pretrained models, inexpensive cloud resources, shared datasets, automated experiment tracking, collaborative software platforms, improved accelerators, and rapidly expanding open-source code. Each can reduce research friction independently of language models. The correct counterfactual is therefore not a static 2013 research process with generative AI switched on or off; it is a technological system in which many complementary inputs have become cheaper and more capable simultaneously.

This matters because complementary technologies can amplify one another. A language model that writes experimental code becomes more useful when mature libraries already expose the relevant operations through simple APIs. AI-assisted literature search becomes more useful when papers are digitally available and machine-readable. An agent capable of designing experiments becomes more productive when cloud compute, pretrained models, standardized datasets, and automated evaluation pipelines are already accessible. Even if recent AI systems accelerate research, the observed output increase may reflect a compound production system rather than an isolated "LLM effect."

A fifth explanation concerns **publication behavior rather than research production**. The number of public artifacts can increase because a larger fraction of completed work is posted as a preprint, because researchers split projects differently across manuscripts, because submission costs fall, because publication incentives intensify, or because institutions increasingly reward visible output. An increase in papers is therefore not necessarily an equal increase in underlying research activity. The distinction is particularly important for arXiv, where a change in preprint adoption can raise repository volume even if the number of completed research projects changes less.

The converse is possible as well. Lower manuscript-production costs could cause previously completed but unwritten work to become visible. In that case AI would increase measured publication output even if it had little effect on scientific discovery itself. This would still be a genuine productivity effect at the dissemination stage, but it would be different from accelerating theorem discovery, experimental design, or conceptual innovation. The research production function must therefore be decomposed before asking which part AI has changed.

Mathematics provides a useful comparison precisely because several of these machine-learning-specific explanations become weaker. Epoch's dataset concerns papers whose primary arXiv classification is mathematics rather than papers submitted to an AI conference. Across matched January-August periods, the number of mathematics preprints examined increased from 26,620 in 2025 to 35,678 in 2026, or **34.0%**, while papers explicitly acknowledging AI use increased from 185 to 3,407.[^the-research-explosion-epoch-august] Mathematics has not suddenly become a field whose entire subject matter is new AI models, so this observation weakens the narrow claim that the only phenomenon occurring is an explosion of research *about* AI.

It does not, however, turn mathematics into a valid control group. Mathematical output can grow for unrelated reasons; field composition can change; arXiv usage can change; AI-related mathematics itself can expand; and the 2025–2026 interval is too short to infer a stable counterfactual trend. The simultaneous 34% increase in preprint volume and dramatic increase in disclosed AI use is therefore evidence that deserves explanation, not an experiment that identifies AI's causal contribution.

A sixth alternative is **compositional change in the author population**. Suppose most established mathematicians retained roughly their previous workflows while a new population of AI-intensive authors entered arXiv and produced papers at unusually high rates. Aggregate AI acknowledgments could then rise without indicating a comparable technological change among existing researchers. Epoch explicitly tests part of this hypothesis by restricting its analysis to papers containing at least one "established author," defined using a prior mathematics-publication history. It reports that the monthly AI-acknowledgment rate for this restricted population remains within **1.5 percentage points** of the overall series.[^the-research-explosion-epoch-august]

That result eliminates neither selection effects nor causal ambiguity, but it is informative. The rise in disclosed AI participation cannot be attributed solely to a peripheral influx of newly appearing AI-dependent authors. Researchers with established publication histories are participating in approximately the same adoption trend. The evidence therefore supports diffusion of AI into the incumbent research population, although it still does not tell us how much additional research each adopter produces because of it.

The most important measurement alternative is **disclosure behavior itself**. Epoch's methodology observes acknowledged AI use, not all AI use. An author who uses a model extensively but does not disclose it appears in the dataset as a non-user; an author who begins reporting a type of assistance that had previously gone unmentioned creates an apparent increase even if their underlying behavior has not changed. Epoch explicitly cautions that its series therefore reflects changes in disclosure behavior as well as changes in AI adoption.[^the-research-explosion-epoch-august][^the-research-explosion-epoch-methodology]

This is particularly important around 2026 because disclosure requirements and community expectations themselves are changing. ICLR 2027, for example, requires authors to disclose LLM use in the manuscript and submission form.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-authors] As disclosure becomes institutionalized, observed acknowledgment rates can increase mechanically. The true fraction of researchers using AI could simultaneously be much higher than the measured fraction, while the measured *growth rate* could exceed the growth rate of underlying use. Voluntary acknowledgments are therefore neither a lower-bound time series with a constant bias nor an unbiased estimator of adoption.

There is also a selection effect in what gets observed. The Epoch sample contains research that reached arXiv. If AI helps researchers abandon weak projects earlier, improve unsuccessful projects until they become publishable, or produce more failed experiments without posting them, those changes remain invisible. Conversely, if AI makes it much cheaper to convert a marginal idea into a polished preprint, the observable dataset will disproportionately capture that margin. Publication data reveal the output of a selection process, not the complete distribution of research attempts behind it.

These alternatives can be organized as a causal decomposition. An observed increase in candidate research $N$ can result from changes in at least five latent factors:

$$
\Delta N
=
f(
\Delta A,\,
\Delta O,\,
\Delta I,\,
\Delta P,\,
\Delta T
),
$$ {#eq-the-research-explosion-causal-decomposition}

where $A$ represents the active research population, $O$ the opportunity set of research questions, $I$ the non-AI research infrastructure available to researchers, $P$ publication and submission behavior, and $T$ the productivity effect of AI tools. This is a schematic relationship rather than an estimable equation: the variables interact, are only partially observable, and cannot be additively decomposed from the aggregate data available here. Its purpose is to state the identification problem explicitly. Observing $\Delta N>0$ while $T$ is increasing does not identify the partial contribution of $T$.

A credible estimate of that contribution would require evidence closer to the researcher or project level. Useful designs would compare the same researchers before and after adoption, exploit plausibly exogenous differences in access to capable systems, measure differential productivity across tasks with different degrees of AI exposure, or construct longitudinal panels controlling for career stage, field, collaboration structure, and pre-existing productivity. The outcomes should also extend beyond manuscript count to completion time, abandoned projects, result quality, acceptance, reproducibility, novelty, and later scientific reuse. Without such a counterfactual, aggregate growth remains descriptively important but causally underdetermined.

The evidence nevertheless rules out several excessively simple interpretations. The explosion did **not** begin with generative AI: both ICLR and AI publication volume were already rising strongly beforehand. It is **not** adequately explained by conference growth alone: increases also appear in preprint repositories and across multiple venues. The extraordinary rise in disclosed AI use in mathematics is **not** solely an influx of new authors: Epoch observes nearly the same adoption pattern among established researchers. And the acknowledgment curve cannot simply be interpreted as latent AI adoption because reporting behavior is itself changing.

What remains is a narrower and more defensible hypothesis. Generative AI has entered an already rapidly expanding research system whose population, opportunity set, infrastructure, and publication channels were themselves growing. It is now being used by established researchers across activities that directly enter the research production function, while candidate output is accelerating in several domains and evaluation institutions are reporting capacity pressure. The available data do not determine how much of that acceleration AI caused. They establish instead the conditions under which an AI-driven productivity effect could become large—and make identifying that effect one of the empirical problems that the next generation of science-of-science research will have to solve.

[^the-research-explosion-ai-index-publications]: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. (2026). **AI Index Report 2026 — Research and Development: Publications**. Using OpenAlex and the CSO Classifier, the report estimates that AI publications increased from approximately 102,000 in 2013 to about 258,000 in 2024 and that AI-related work accounted for approximately 40.9% of computer-science publications in 2024. [Research report](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/research-and-development)

## What happens when research supply becomes effectively abundant

If candidate research becomes much cheaper to produce, the immediate consequence is not that science becomes abundant in every meaningful sense. Experiments can remain expensive, specialized data scarce, laboratory infrastructure limited, and genuinely important ideas rare. What can become abundant is a narrower object: **candidate claims sufficiently developed to demand evaluation**. Once their supply grows faster than the capacity available to examine them carefully, the architecture of scientific selection must change.

The traditional publication pipeline contains an implicit upstream filter. Before a researcher can ask a conference or journal to evaluate a claim, enough effort must normally be invested to develop the idea, perform the analysis or experiments, reconstruct the literature, prepare figures, write the manuscript, and satisfy submission requirements. That cost does not guarantee quality, but it suppresses some fraction of possible submissions. When several of those activities become cheaper, the implicit filter weakens. More projects can survive long enough to reach the explicit filtering institutions downstream.

The first response is therefore **admission control**. ICLR's 2027 policies make this transition unusually visible. The Program Chairs explicitly describe the new rules as effective submission "rate limits": authors may appear on no more than twenty submissions, while groups composed entirely of authors without prior publication at major relevant venues face a much tighter constraint; the formal author guidelines additionally connect submission rights to reciprocal-review obligations.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-rate-limits][^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-guidelines] Whatever one thinks about the particular design of those rules, their function is clear. The system is no longer assuming that every technically admissible candidate can consume an unconstrained amount of downstream evaluation capacity.

This is a structural change. In a low-volume regime, peer review can behave approximately as a universal service: submit a compliant paper and the institution attempts to allocate qualified reviewers to it. In a sufficiently high-volume regime, evaluation itself must first be allocated. The institution therefore acquires a problem logically prior to reviewing individual claims:

> Which candidates deserve the scarce resources required to determine whether they deserve acceptance?

The paradox is only apparent. Selection must begin before full evaluation because full evaluation has itself become the scarce resource.

A simple capacity variable makes the transition explicit. Let $N$ denote the number of candidates seeking evaluation and $E$ the number that can be evaluated at the desired depth with the available resources. Define evaluation coverage as

$$
\gamma
=
\min\left(1,\frac{E}{N}\right).
$$ {#eq-the-research-explosion-evaluation-coverage}

If $N\leq E$, every candidate can in principle receive the intended level of scrutiny and $\gamma=1$. If $N>E$, complete coverage at the same standard becomes impossible unless evaluation capacity expands. The institution must then act on one or more variables: increase $E$, reduce $N$, decrease the average evaluation effort per candidate, lengthen the process, or stratify candidates into different levels of scrutiny.

The distinction between **coverage** and **quality** is essential. A conference can preserve $\gamma=1$ mechanically by assigning fewer minutes of attention to each paper, recruiting less-qualified reviewers, or replacing detailed examination with automated summaries. The arithmetic would still show complete coverage while the epistemic meaning of "reviewed" had changed. A scalable evaluation system must therefore preserve not merely the existence of an evaluation but some minimum standard of expertise, independence, and depth.

This is why ICLR's response operates on several margins simultaneously. Reciprocal reviewing attempts to enlarge $E$ by requiring contributors to supply evaluation labor. Submission limits constrain $N$. Desk rejection permits relatively inexpensive screening before full evaluation. Reviewer-quality policies attempt to prevent nominal increases in reviewing capacity from being purchased through arbitrarily weaker reviews. These mechanisms address different terms of the same problem rather than constituting unrelated administrative rules.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-guidelines][^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-rate-limits]

As supply continues to increase, however, binary admission control is unlikely to be sufficient. A more general architecture is **progressive evaluation**: inexpensive tests are applied broadly, while increasingly expensive forms of scrutiny are reserved for candidates that survive earlier stages. The principle already appears throughout scientific practice. Formatting and policy compliance are checked before substantive review; abstracts support reviewer bidding; reviewers perform the first technical assessment; area chairs integrate reviews; only a subset of results will later receive replication attempts, extensive follow-up, formal verification, or incorporation into textbooks and scientific infrastructure.

Under abundance, this layered structure becomes more important because verification costs differ by orders of magnitude. Checking that references exist is cheap relative to reproducing an experimental result. Running provided code can be cheaper than reconstructing an experiment independently. Checking a formal proof term can be cheaper than determining whether the theorem formalized was the scientifically intended one. Reading a manuscript is cheaper than building another laboratory to reproduce it. Rational allocation therefore sends inexpensive checks across a broad candidate population and reserves costly independent verification for claims whose expected informational value justifies it.

Let evaluation stage $s$ have average cost $c_s$, with candidates surviving that stage with probability $p_s$. If $N_0=N$ candidates enter the system, the expected number reaching stage $s$ is approximately

$$
N_s
=
N \prod_{k=1}^{s} p_k.
$$ {#eq-the-research-explosion-progressive-filtering}

The corresponding expected evaluation resource consumption is

$$
C
=
\sum_{s=0}^{S} N_s c_s.
$$ {#eq-the-research-explosion-filtering-cost}

These equations are schematic rather than a prescription for conference design. Their point is that ordering matters. If inexpensive, sufficiently reliable filters eliminate candidates that clearly fail formal, ethical, provenance, or minimum-quality requirements, expensive expert attention can be concentrated on the remaining claims. Conversely, a weak early filter can propagate an enormous candidate population into later stages and make the entire system infeasible.

Automation is therefore likely to enter evaluation first where the decision criterion is relatively well specified. Software can check formatting requirements, identify duplicate text, validate references, execute tests, inspect metadata, detect some statistical anomalies, compare manuscript versions, and mechanically verify formal proofs. ICLR itself now requires explicit AI-use statements covering a broad range of research tasks, from hypothesis formation and theoretical modeling to implementation, proof assistance, data analysis, and interpretation.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-authors] Such provenance information can become an input to later evaluation because reviewers increasingly need to understand not only the visible result but how it was produced.

The important boundary is between **screening** and **judgment**. Automated screening can answer questions such as whether a DOI resolves, whether reported code executes in a specified environment, whether two numerical tables are internally consistent, or whether a formal object type-checks. Scientific judgment asks different questions: whether the assumptions are sensible, whether the benchmark captures the phenomenon of interest, whether the result is genuinely surprising, whether an apparent novelty matters, whether alternative explanations have been eliminated, or whether finite experimental resources should be spent attempting an independent replication. The former class can often be converted into explicit tests. The latter frequently involves open-ended comparisons against the evolving state of a field.

This difference has consequences for AI-assisted evaluation. If generation and evaluation use similar foundation models, the system can create large quantities of mutually consistent artifacts without generating equivalent independent evidence. A model may produce a claim, another instance of the same model family may review it, and a third may summarize the resulting discussion. Textual agreement among those stages can look like repeated confirmation while sharing common training data, representations, blind spots, or inference errors. Scaling evaluation therefore requires attention not only to how many checks occur but to **how independent their failure modes are**.

For candidate $i$, suppose evaluation channels $1,\ldots,m$ produce apparent confirmations, but let $d_{ij}$ denote the incremental information contributed by channel $j$ conditional on what previous channels have already established. Effective corroboration then depends on the conditional contributions

$$
I_i
=
\sum_{j=1}^{m} d_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-the-research-explosion-incremental-evidence}

not simply on $m$. If several evaluation channels reproduce the same assumptions or systematic error, additional evaluations can have small $d_{ij}$ even though the artifact count continues to rise. Scientific scalability therefore depends partly on preserving **diversity of evidence**, not merely multiplying evaluations.

Provenance becomes more valuable for the same reason. When research artifacts were costly to produce, the finished manuscript contained some weak information about the process behind it: substantial effort had normally been required simply to create the object. As generative systems reduce that cost, polished presentation carries less information about whether a claim was independently derived, carefully tested, copied from an existing source, produced through model assistance, or checked through genuinely separate methods. Evaluation increasingly needs metadata about process as well as access to the final artifact.

ICLR's 2027 AI policy is an early example of this shift. Authors must disclose AI use not merely for prose generation but for substantive activities including developing conceptual frameworks, formulating mathematical claims, contributing to proofs, proposing hypotheses, designing experiments, implementing methods, analyzing data, and interpreting results.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-authors] The policy retains responsibility with the human authors, who are explicitly accountable for falsehoods, plagiarism, or misrepresentations produced through AI assistance. Disclosure does not establish correctness; it improves the inspectability of the production path.

The same principle appears on the review side. ICLR allows limited AI assistance in reviews but requires disclosure and, when an LLM contributes to review text, preservation of the reviewer's original self-written assessment and relevant model interactions.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-reviewers] This policy creates a provenance chain between human judgment and machine-mediated presentation. Its importance increases precisely when generating a plausible review becomes cheap, because the finished review text alone becomes weaker evidence that an independent expert actually performed the underlying evaluation.

Research abundance can therefore generate a second institutional transition: from evaluating **artifacts** to evaluating **artifact-plus-provenance**. For computational work this may include code, environments, datasets, random seeds, model versions, prompts, agent traces, and execution logs. In mathematics it can include informal arguments, formal statements, proof objects, dependency graphs, model interaction histories, and independent theorem checking. In empirical science it may include protocols, preregistration, laboratory records, raw data, analysis pipelines, and independent replication. The relevant provenance structure differs by field, but the underlying reason is the same: when producing the visible surface becomes cheaper, evidence about the process behind it becomes more informative.

Abundance also changes the role of **ranking**. Under scarcity of candidate research, the fundamental problem is obtaining enough worthwhile results. Under candidate abundance, the research community must increasingly decide which valid or potentially valid results deserve scarce downstream attention. Correctness becomes one filter among several. Novelty, expected importance, uncertainty reduction, potential for reuse, replication value, and relation to unresolved questions become allocation criteria because it is impossible to investigate everything with equal depth.

This has an uncomfortable implication: a future research system could contain more correct results than any human community can meaningfully absorb. Mathematics provides the cleanest limiting case. If theorem-generating systems eventually produce millions of formally valid new statements, mechanical correctness alone will no longer determine what enters the active body of mathematics. The scarce operations will include discovering which statements compress existing knowledge, reveal reusable structure, answer important questions, connect previously separate domains, or enable further reasoning. Selection becomes partly a problem of **scientific significance under abundance**.

The same phenomenon already exists in less extreme form in empirical machine learning. A very large number of experiments can be technically valid while varying hyperparameters, architectures, datasets, prompts, agent designs, or evaluation procedures. The central problem is not whether each individual experiment can be executed but whether its result changes an informed observer's beliefs about anything sufficiently important. Cheap experimentation increases the value of mechanisms that detect redundancy and identify experiments with high expected information gain.



The limiting resource is consequently not publication space in the old physical sense. Digital repositories can store millions of additional papers at comparatively low cost. Nor is it necessarily the mechanical ability to produce reviews, summaries, or replications, because AI may make each of those artifacts cheaper as well. The deeper scarcity is the capacity to allocate **credible, independent, appropriately specialized attention** to the claims for which such attention has the highest scientific value.

This changes what a scalable scientific infrastructure must optimize. A system designed primarily for scarcity of candidate work seeks to encourage production and disseminate results. A system designed for candidate abundance must additionally perform admission control, progressive filtering, provenance capture, redundancy detection, reviewer matching, independence management, prioritization, and selective escalation to expensive verification. The scientific institution becomes partly an allocation mechanism for epistemic resources.

The key question is therefore not whether the research system can technically accept another million papers. It can. The question is whether it can preserve a meaningful mapping between the growing supply of candidate claims and the finite resources required to determine which claims are reliable, which are new, which are important, and which deserve further investigation. Once candidate generation approaches abundance, **selection itself becomes a central scientific technology**.

## Measuring scientific productivity in the AI era

Paper counts become less informative as measures of scientific productivity when the production process changes rapidly. A paper written with no AI assistance and a paper whose literature search, code, formalization, and prose were substantially AI-assisted each contribute exactly one unit to a publication count, even though their labor inputs and production technologies differ. The problem is not unique to AI—papers have always varied enormously in effort and importance—but rapid technological change makes the instability of the unit harder to ignore.

A more useful framework separates stages that conventional bibliometrics compresses. Candidate production can be measured through submissions or preprints; evaluation through reviews, formal checks, and reproduction attempts; selection through editorial or conference decisions; assimilation through reuse in later research, software, formal libraries, experiments, or practice; and durability through survival under later scrutiny. None is a sufficient measure of knowledge, but separating them prevents growth at one stage from being mistaken for growth at all stages.

@tbl-the-research-explosion-productivity-measures applies that distinction to the evidence available here.

| Quantity | Observed measure | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Candidate production | 19,525 valid, format-compliant ICLR 2026 submissions | Scale entering the review process | Correctness, novelty, reproducibility, or importance |
| Realized review activity | 76,139 ICLR 2026 reviews | Scale of recorded evaluation work | Equal depth, independence, or reliability of reviews |
| Decision throughput | 13,763 ICLR 2026 accept-or-reject decisions | Number reaching a conference decision | Long-run validity or scientific impact |
| Acknowledged AI participation | 25.25% of Epoch's August 2026 mathematics sample | Disclosed AI participation in research workflows | Total AI use or a causal productivity effect |
| Acknowledged substantial research use | 5.86% of Epoch's August 2026 mathematics sample | Disclosed AI contributions meeting Epoch's stricter research classification | Independent proof that AI originated or correctly established the result |
| Scientific assimilation | Not measured by these datasets | — | Whether a result is reproduced, reused, understood, or durable |

: Different stages of the research process require different productivity measures. {#tbl-the-research-explosion-productivity-measures}

The table exposes why an increase in submissions cannot by itself establish an equivalent increase in knowledge. Reviews measure evaluation activity but not necessarily evaluation quality; acceptances measure institutional selection but not long-run validity; citations measure attention and reuse imperfectly and are affected by field size; downloads measure access; and formal verification, where available, establishes particular forms of correctness without determining significance. Scientific productivity is therefore intrinsically multidimensional.

A conceptual refinement of the earlier validation equation can represent redundancy as well as correctness. Let $q_i$ again denote the probability that candidate $i$ survives relevant validation, and let $w_i$ denote its incremental scientific value conditional on knowledge already available. Then

$$
K^\ast = \sum_{i=1}^{N} q_i w_i.
$${#eq-the-research-explosion-effective-knowledge}

Neither $q_i$ nor $w_i$ is proposed here as an operational bibliometric score. The equation instead identifies two dimensions that raw counts omit. A research system can generate more correct results while producing little additional information if those results are highly redundant, and it can produce fewer artifacts while increasing epistemic productivity if the artifacts are better verified or more consequential.

This distinction changes how AI productivity should be evaluated. If AI doubles the number of manuscripts but leaves validated non-redundant contributions almost unchanged, artifact productivity has increased more than epistemic productivity. If AI allows researchers to perform stronger robustness checks, formalize arguments, explore harder conjectures, or reproduce results without increasing paper counts, scientific productivity may rise while conventional output metrics barely move. Measuring the AI era therefore requires observing what happens after generation rather than assuming that generation is the endpoint.

## From a scarcity of research to a scarcity of trust

The strongest conclusion supported by the evidence is not that AI has caused the research explosion. ICLR's growth clearly predates the current generative-AI era, and neither conference statistics nor Epoch's acknowledgment data identify a causal counterfactual. The stronger factual statement is that candidate research is expanding extraordinarily quickly, disclosed AI participation is simultaneously rising rapidly in mathematics, and ICLR reports that AI-generated material is already affecting both submissions and reviews.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2026-retrospective][^the-research-explosion-epoch-august] The causal share attributable to AI remains unknown; the institutional collision between high-volume production and finite evaluation capacity is already observable.

That collision makes trust a systems problem. Scientific confidence does not arise merely because a claim has been evaluated many times; it depends on the quality and independence of those evaluations. If $m$ assessments examine a claim and $d_j$ represents the incremental independent evidentiary contribution of assessment $j$ conditional on the preceding assessments, then a conceptual quantity for independent verification is

$$
V_{\mathrm{ind}} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} d_j.
$${#eq-the-research-explosion-independent-verification}

As with the earlier epistemic quantities, this is not an operational score. It formalizes a distinction that becomes important when AI participates in both generation and checking. Five evaluations based on genuinely different evidence or methods can add substantial confidence; five evaluations reproducing the same model's assumptions or systematic error can generate five artifacts while adding much less independent evidence.

ICLR's reviewer policy implicitly recognizes this distinction. The conference permits limited AI assistance with review writing but requires disclosure, the reviewer's original self-written assessment, and the relevant model interactions; it also retains disciplinary mechanisms for hallucinated or misleading AI-generated review content.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-reviewers] The scarce object is not review prose but accountable judgment. Similarly, ICLR's author policy requires explicit disclosure of LLM use because provenance becomes more valuable when the visible artifact conveys less information about how it was produced.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-authors]

Mathematics makes the provenance problem especially clear. A proof assistant can provide strong evidence that a formal term satisfies a stated theorem within a trusted formal system, but this does not by itself establish that the theorem captures the intended informal claim, that its assumptions are scientifically appropriate, that the result is novel, or that it is important. The *AI and the transformation of mathematics* series develops this migration of scarcity from proof production toward formalization, verification, interpretation, provenance, and mathematical significance.[^the-research-explosion-montano-series] The same architecture is beginning to appear more broadly: as candidate artifacts become cheaper, the path by which a result was generated and checked becomes part of the evidence needed to trust it.

A mature AI-era research infrastructure would therefore make the evidentiary path increasingly inspectable. Depending on the field, that path can include data provenance, executable analysis, code and environment capture, model and tool disclosure, formal checks, independent reproduction, reviewer assessments, corrections, and downstream reuse. None of these mechanisms guarantees truth, and not every field can use the same combination, but they move measurement away from the surface appearance of a paper and toward the processes that support its claims.

The research explosion should consequently be understood as a change in the relative scarcity structure of science. Many fields still suffer from too little funding, too few experiments, insufficient data, inadequate infrastructure, and too few researchers; nothing in this analysis implies that research is globally abundant. The narrower claim is that, in domains where AI and associated infrastructure substantially reduce the cost of generating candidate work, the marginal bottleneck can move downstream. Producing another plausible artifact becomes easier than establishing that it is correct, non-redundant, important, independently supported, and worthy of finite expert attention.

ICLR already provides hard evidence of that transition. Its valid submission count increased by 68.3% from 2025 to 2026, while its organizers describe review capacity as strained and have introduced explicit limits and reciprocal-review requirements.[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2026-fact-sheet][^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-guidelines] Epoch independently reports that one quarter of the mathematics preprints it examined in August 2026 acknowledged some AI use and 5.86% acknowledged AI contributions meeting its substantial-research criterion, while warning that disclosure is an imperfect measure of underlying use.[^the-research-explosion-epoch-august] Neither observation proves that AI caused the other. Together, however, they describe a research system in which the production technology is changing at the same time that the cost of evaluating its output is becoming institutionally salient.

If that pattern persists, the decisive scientific infrastructure of the AI era will not be defined only by its capacity to generate more hypotheses, proofs, experiments, code, or papers. Its value will increasingly depend on whether it can preserve provenance, support independent verification, expose uncertainty, identify redundancy, allocate expert attention, and distinguish a large supply of plausible claims from a durable body of knowledge. The research explosion is therefore not simply a story about abundance. It is a transition from a system in which producing research was a dominant scarcity toward one in which **credible trust in research may become the harder resource to scale**.

(2016). **Welcome to ICLR 2016!** The official opening presentation reports conference-track submissions of 67 in 2013, 87 in 2014, 143 in 2015, and more than 265 in 2016; the 2016 value is explicitly marked as conference-track submissions only. [Official presentation](https://dev.iclr.cc/archive/www/lib/exe/fetch.php%3Fmedia%3Diclr2016%3Aopening.pdf)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2023-fact-sheet]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2023). **ICLR 2023 Fact Sheet**. The official fact sheet reports 4,938 submissions, 1,574 accepted papers, and 5,734 reviewers. [Official fact sheet](https://media.iclr.cc/Conferences/ICLR2023/ICLR2023-Fact_Sheet.pdf)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2025-fact-sheet]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2025). **ICLR 2025 Fact Sheet**. The official fact sheet reports 11,603 submissions and 3,704 accepted papers and states that submissions increased by 4,341 from 2024; it also reports 18,325 reviewers. [Official fact sheet](https://media.iclr.cc/Conferences/ICLR2025/ICLR2025_Fact_Sheet.pdf)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2026-fact-sheet]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2026). **ICLR 2026 Fact Sheet**. The official fact sheet reports 19,525 submissions and 5,357 accepted papers, compared with 11,603 submissions and 3,704 accepted papers in 2025; it records 7,922 additional submissions and 21,674 reviewers compared with 18,325 in 2025. [Official fact sheet](https://media.iclr.cc/Conferences/ICLR2026/ICLR2026_Fact_Sheet.pdf)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2026-retrospective]: ICLR 2026 Program Chairs. (2026). **A Retrospective on the ICLR 2026 Review Process**. The retrospective reports 19,525 valid, format-compliant submissions, 779 desk rejections, 5,042 withdrawals, 13,763 submissions receiving accept-or-reject decisions, and 76,139 reviews from 18,054 participating reviewers. It also discusses LLM-related problems in submissions and reviews. [Official retrospective](https://blog.iclr.cc/2026/03/31/a-retrospective-on-the-iclr-2026-review-process/)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-rate-limits]: Andreas, J., Van den Broeck, G., Risteski, A., & Yu, S. (2026). **Submission policies for ICLR 2027**. The program chairs describe the new rules as effective submission rate limits; report that about 20% of ICLR 2026 submissions had no reciprocal reviewer, about 40% of that group involved authors submitting multiple such papers, and fewer than 0.2% of authors submitted more than twenty papers; and state that many low-performing submissions in the no-reviewer group involved low-quality or AI-generated content while others were excellent and accepted. [Official announcement](https://blog.iclr.cc/2026/09/02/submission-policies-for-iclr-2027/)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-guidelines]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2026). **ICLR 2027 Author Guidelines**. The guidelines state that rapid submission growth has begun to strain the review system, impose a twenty-paper coauthorship ceiling, restrict papers with no eligible reciprocal reviewer, and require reviewing service from sufficiently high-volume submitters. [Official guidelines](https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2027/AuthorGuidelines)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2027-call]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2026). **ICLR 2027 Call for Papers**. The call gives an abstract deadline of September 18, 2026 and a paper deadline of September 25, 2026 and defines ICLR's broad current subject scope. [Official call for papers](https://www.iclr.cc/Conferences/2027/CallForPapers)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-authors]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2026). **ICLR 2027 AI Policy for Authors**. The policy states that LLMs are increasingly used in research workflows ranging from proof formulation to table formatting and requires authors to disclose their use in both the manuscript and submission form. [Official policy](https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2027/AIPolicyForAuthors)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-ai-reviewers]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2026). **Policy on LLM use for writing reviews or meta-reviews**. ICLR permits limited AI assistance with review writing but requires disclosure, the reviewer's original self-written assessment, and relevant model interactions; false or misleading AI-generated content can lead to disciplinary consequences. [Official policy](https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2027/AIPolicyForReviewers)

[^the-research-explosion-epoch-august]: Abrishami, T. (2026). **In August, 25% of math preprints acknowledged AI use, up from 4% in April**. Epoch reports monthly mathematics-preprint denominators and AI-acknowledgment counts from January 2025 through August 2026. In August 2026, 1,453 of 5,754 examined papers acknowledged AI use and 337, or 5.86%, acknowledged substantial-research use. Epoch explicitly notes that voluntary disclosure makes the series sensitive to changes in disclosure behavior. [Data analysis](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/math-preprints-disclosed-ai-use)

[^the-research-explosion-epoch-methodology]: Epoch AI. (2026). **AI Use in Math Research Documentation**. Epoch sources mathematics metadata from arXiv, assigns papers by first submission date and primary mathematics category, classifies acknowledged uses including research, writing, code and computation, literature review, and formalization, and applies stricter validation to research classifications. Its documented audit reports 93% agreement at the research-category level for the audited research classifications. [Dataset documentation](https://epoch.ai/data/arxiv-documentation)

[^the-research-explosion-chatgpt-release]: OpenAI. (2022). **Introducing ChatGPT**. The original announcement is dated November 30, 2022 and describes the public research preview of ChatGPT. [Official announcement](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/)

[^the-research-explosion-montano-series]: Montano, A. (2026). **AI and the transformation of mathematics**. The series examines proof abundance, machine-scale mathematical search, formalization, automated proof checking, provenance, interpretation, and the infrastructure required to maintain mathematical trust as AI participates more deeply in research. [Article series](https://4m4.it/series/ai-and-the-transformation-of-mathematics/)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-intermediate-history]: The historical series reports 507 submissions in 2017, 981 in 2018, and 1,591 in 2019. These observations are useful for reconstructing the annual trajectory, but they come from a historical conference-statistics compilation rather than a single standardized ICLR statistical release, so their counting conventions should not automatically be assumed to be identical to those of later ICLR fact sheets. [Historical statistics](https://csconfstats.xoveexu.com/conferences/iclr/)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2021-retrospective]: Hofmann, K., Titov, I., Murray, N., & Oh, A. (2021). **ICLR 2021 — A retrospective from the program committee**. The ICLR program committee reports 3,014 full submissions for ICLR 2021, compared with 2,604 full submissions in 2020. [Official retrospective](https://iclr-conf.medium.com/iclr-2021-a-retrospective-from-the-program-committee-26a1132cfd96)

[^the-research-explosion-iclr-2022-fact-sheet]: International Conference on Learning Representations. (2022). **ICLR 2022 Fact Sheet**.
